summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base for managing IPv4 multicast routing, independent of the multicast routing protocol in use. It was later replaced by RFC 5132.

plainLanguage.summary: This lets management tools look at how group-delivery traffic is being routed, no matter which method is used.

questions: how to monitor multicast routing with snmp
subtitle: SNMP management of IPv4 multicast routing across different protocols

tldr.problem: Network administrators need a standard way to monitor and manage IPv4 multicast routing, regardless of which multicast routing protocol (DVMRP, PIM, CBT, etc.) a router uses.
tldr.mechanism: This MIB defines a collection of managed objects that describe multicast routing information, including active routes, next hops, interfaces, and scope boundaries, all accessible via SNMP.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can now query any router for its multicast state in a protocol-independent way, enabling consistent network management. The RFC was later replaced by RFC 5132 with expanded functionality.

facts.label: MIB tables
facts.value: 5 (Route, Next Hop, Interface, Boundary, Scope Name)

today: RFC 2932 is an Internet Standard and was obsoleted by RFC 5132, which adds support for IPv6 multicast and extends the IPv4 management information. While RFC 2932 itself is now Historic, the core concepts of protocol-independent multicast routing management remain valid.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The IPv4 Multicast Routing MIB defines objects for managing IP multicast routing in IPv4 networks. Multicast is the one-to-many delivery of packets to multiple groups of receivers. A key feature of this MIB is that it is protocol-independent: it works with any multicast routing protocol (such as DVMRP, PIM-SM, PIM-DM, or CBT) without requiring protocol-specific extensions.

Unlike unicast routing, where packets flow from one source to one destination, multicast routing tracks group memberships and replication trees. The MIB provides visibility into how a router forwards packets sent by a source to a multicast group, independent of the underlying protocol used to compute those routes.
sections.plainLanguage: Multicast is sending a message to a bunch of people at once, not just one. This describes how to ask a router which groups it knows about and where it sends their messages.

sections.title: The MIB Tables and Scalar
sections.content:
The MIB defines one scalar object and five tables. The scalar, ipMRouteEnable, turns multicast routing on or off on a router. The five tables are:

  • IP Multicast Route Table: Contains entries for each (source, group) pair known to the router, recording the incoming interface, active time, and packet counters.
  • IP Multicast Routing Next Hop Table: Lists the outgoing interfaces and next-hop addresses for each multicast route, along with the forwarding state (pruned or active).
  • IP Multicast Routing Interface Table: Provides per-interface configuration and statistics, including TTL thresholds and multicast packet counters.
  • IP Multicast Scope Boundary Table: Configures administratively scoped multicast boundaries to prevent certain group addresses from leaving a network region.
  • IP Multicast Scope Name Table: Maps scoped address ranges to human-readable names in multiple languages.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a spreadsheet for each part of how multicast works: one for the groups, one for where to send them, one for each cable, one for barriers, and one for names.

sections.title: Table Structure and Objects
sections.content:
Each table entry is indexed by keys that uniquely identify a multicast route or interface. The Route Table uses (group address, source address, source mask) as its index, allowing a router to track distinct routes for different source networks sending to the same group.

Each entry includes counters for packets and octets forwarded, information about the upstream neighbor (the interface from which traffic arrives), and the multicast routing protocol that learned the route (DVMRP, PIM, CBT, etc.). For high-speed interfaces, the MIB also provides 64-bit octet counters to prevent overflow on links faster than 20 Mbps.
sections.plainLanguage: Each row in the table remembers who sent the message, who wants it, how many people got it, and which method was used to figure out the path.

sections.title: Security and Scope Boundaries
sections.content:
The Scope Boundary Table enforces administratively scoped multicast, a mechanism defined in RFC 2365 to restrict multicast traffic to specific organizational domains (using address ranges 239.0.0.0/8). Operators can configure a router to prevent traffic for certain groups from forwarding out specified interfaces.

From a security perspective, read access to these objects reveals which groups are active and which sources are sending to them. Write access allows operators to modify routing behavior, including disabling multicast routing entirely or changing TTL thresholds. SNMPv3 with its User-based Security Model and view-based access control is recommended to protect this sensitive configuration data.
sections.plainLanguage: Some multicast groups are only meant for your building, not the whole company. You can set rules to keep those messages inside, and you need to guard this carefully so only the right person can change it.

sections.title: Protocol-Independent Design
sections.content:
This MIB is deliberately protocol-agnostic. It does not include objects specific to DVMRP, PIM, or other multicast routing protocols. Routers implementing those protocols can expose their own specialized managed objects in separate MIBs while using the standard objects here.

The MIB works with both SMIv1 and SMIv2 (though the document specifies SMIv2). Routers may support only a subset of the objects based on their capabilities; for example, only interfaces faster than 20 Mbps are required to support the high-capacity counter objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a separate instruction manual for each type of router, this is a basic manual that works with all of them. If a router has special features, it can add extra pages.
